articles.title: Monster Mia review – kooky kid discovers school of beastly besties in wholesome Halloween fun
articles.summary: A scrappy girl discovers her tribe – which includes a vegan vampire – at a school for top scarers in this entertaining pre-teen animation. In films, twins are usually written as either identical personalities or complete and total opposites, and it’s the latter dynamic that’s at work in this…
body: Scrappy Mia is, naturally, the protagonist of this film, and it’s not too long before she finds herself accidentally enrolled in Rotwood Academy, a school for monsters who would be shocked to discover a human in their midst; from their point of view, humans are brutal, cold-blooded creatures, best avoided, who prefer – ugh! – cupcakes to grave-worms. Mia quickly buddies up with some misfits including a vegan vampire, and the stage is thus set for some Addams Family Lite hijinks, with culture clash comedy highlighting the difference between monster norms and human ways providing much of the humour.

The underlying message that we shouldn’t be scared of difference is swiftly established as the major moral theme and while this is not exactly totally original, it proves distinctive enough to entertain its target audience. The message might be hammered home with all the subtlety of a croquet mallet to the head, but – what the hell – it is at least a wholesome philosophy, wrapped in palatable packaging. The Halloween timing of the release should help it connect enjoyably enough with younger spooky-season thrill-seekers.

articles.title: Hollywood AI-listers: is the technology ready to rival flesh-and-blood film stars?
articles.summary: As a freaky Val Kilmer doppelganger stars in a new western and faux starlet Tilly Norwood is set for her feature debut, experts are split on whether mainstream adoption is a long way down the line – or just around the corner.
body: ‘D on’t fear the dead – and don’t fear me.” An exact facsimile of a young Val Kilmer, not quite dead and not quite alive, utters that baiting line in the trailer for the new western As Deep as the Grave. Director Coerte Voorhees knows exactly what he is doing – this is an AI-created version of the late actor, approved by his family but bringing with it a heap of controversy about whether such technology could make flesh-and-blood thespians redundant.

Not just yet, judging by the extended glimpse of the film released earlier this year: it looks like a thirtysomething Kilmer, if a robot version had been sent back to the 1920s American wilderness by Skynet and, as well as being strangely rigid, had forgotten to download his voice, let alone his signature air of spacey shrewdness. Kilmer’s estate signed off on it, citing his enthusiasm for new technology that expands storytelling, but surely he would have been dismayed by this freaky doppelganger.

articles.title: ‘Big Boys Don’t Cry’ Director Muhammad Mustapha Talks Masculinity Ahead of El Gouna Premiere: ‘The Only Emotion Men Are Allowed to Express Is Anger’
articles.summary: Egyptian filmmaker Muhammad Mustapha’s “Big Boys Don’t Cry” follows a group of Cairo bodybuilders and nightclub bouncers, offering a view into how men understand and perform masculinity.
body: Mustapha distinguishes that curiosity from a desire to investigate something he saw as inherently wrong. When he began the project in 2016, he approached it as an anthropological and sociological study of masculinity and how it is expressed in different contexts.

His own upbringing gave him a point of reference. Mustapha grew up in what he describes as a “local” Cairo neighborhood, where he was surrounded by its masculine codes. As a studious “nerd,” he could be seen as less masculine there. But when he entered dental school, the same behavior could instead make him appear loud or vulgar.
That contrast helped him recognize how masculinity could shift according to context, a fact he also saw among the men he was observing.
“How they perform their masculinity on stage is different than in front of the pub, is different than when he is addressing a problem, different than when he is with his family,” he says.

articles.title: The Cycle review – forensic scientist autopsies her dad in grisly psychodrama that turns supernatural
articles.summary: Tense story fritters away initial levels interest as generic horrors eclipse offbeat family dynamic. This gloomy-toned film takes its sweet time revealing its genre nature, emerging as a proper horror flick more than halfway in with a detailed transformation sequence.
body: It’s a shame that the hardcore creature-feature stuff is a letdown because the drama leading up to it isn’t bad. We start with a forensic science expert called Meg (Deborah Ann Woll), a young woman whose shiny hair and perky professional attitude disguises a steely composure and strong stomach that’s not in the slightest bit discombobulated by all the rotting, decomposing flesh she deals with on the daily.

Meg is not in the least upset, or so it seems, when one of the bodies found at a murder site is revealed by DNA tests to be that of her own father, Peter (played in flashbacks by David Myers Gregory), who went missing when Meg was but a girl. Nor is she hesitant to pick up her scalpel and commence an autopsy on Dad’s corpse, finding strange anomalies on his anatomy, including evidence of gunshots and multiple ribs that broke and healed over the years. Father and son police officers Marks (Jeffrey Donovan) and Ian (Will Hochman) look on aghast but sort of impressed.

body: Well, it’s fantastic for us to have Frank Miller here. He loves Italy; he loves Lucca, and he’s returning for what I believe is the fourth or fifth time. We couldn’t be happier. Frank truly embodies the values of Lucca and the types of genre we love. We also have talents like Kore-eda [Hirokazu] who this year attended the Cannes Film Festival for one type of project [“Sheep in the Box”], but is then coming to Lucca for another [“Look Back”]. He really represents the multimedia nature of Lucca.

articles.title: ‘Lilly,’ Starring Patricia Clarkson, to Open London’s Women and the World Intl. Film Festival
articles.summary: Rachel Feldman’s “Lilly,” starring Patricia Clarkson, will open the third edition of the Women and the World International Film Festival, which runs in London from Nov. 5-12. Highlights of the program, which puts women’s authorship at its center, include the world premiere of Sigrid Andrea P.
body: “We believe there should simply be more films by women in the world – and more opportunities for those films to reach audiences. Celebrating women is important, but celebration alone is not enough. We want to support them, advocate for them and connect their work directly with audiences and the international film industry.”

The jury includes David Gyasi, British actor and producer; Olwen Fouéré, Irish actor, writer and director; MyAnna Buring, British-Swedish actor; Elena Andreicheva, documentary filmmaker and producer; Denise Parkinson, VP, sales and marketing global, Variety; David Martinez, film publicity executive; Rebecca del Tufo, co-founder and co-director, ScreenCraft Works; and Victoria Emslie, British actor and producer.

In addition to the screening program, WWIFF said it is expanding its efforts to provide a platform for emerging filmmakers and creative talent through collaborations with University College London, LAMDA, Film London and BFI Network.
The festival’s 2025 edition attracted 2,450 attendees and closed with the U.K. premiere of Scarlett Johansson’s directorial debut “Eleanor the Great.”

articles.title: Locals honoured in Notting Hill Frieze exhibition
articles.summary: London street artist Endless's new installation, Endless Frieze, includes buildings and street scenes.
body: A fourth-generation Portobello market trader, a Notting Hill Carnival stalwart and fashion icon known locally as "Notting Hill's best dressed man" are among the people featured in a new artwork by street artist Endless, about Notting Hill's identity.
The installation, Endless Frieze, displays local buildings and street scenes celebrating the west London neighbourhood as part of the annual art fair Frieze London.
Guests and celebrities specifically chosen for their contribution to the area's identity were photographed during a live event on Friday and now feature as part of the exhibition.
The work is "about the community and bringing them into the art world and into my world," Endless said.

articles.title: 'Alice Cooper is a character, like Jekyll and Hyde'
articles.summary: Alice Cooper reflects on faith, fame and addiction ahead of his Wolverhampton book tour appearance.
body: Rock legend Alice Cooper has opened up about his redemption arc from the stage to the church ahead of a book tour pit stop in Wolverhampton.
"It's such a strange life that I had because I was the prodigal son. I grew up in a Christian church, went as far away as you can, then came back," he told BBC Radio WM.

It comes after the singer-songwriter published his autobiography, Devil on My Shoulder, earlier this month, detailing the highs and lows of his nearly six-decade career that earned him the title of the Godfather of Shock Rock.
He is set to appear at the University of Wolverhampton at The Halls on Tuesday.

articles.title: ‘Lex Julia’ Is a Post-#MeToo Suspense Drama Unfolding on an Island (Exclusive Tallinn Trailer)
articles.summary: Laura Hyppönen's film with Rea Lest, Christian Hillborg and Jessica Grabowsky, which will also screen at Mar del Plata, explores the conflicting experiences of a rape victim, the alleged perpetrator and his wife.
body: Trauma, drama, emotion and suspense are among the ingredients that make for a visceral mix in Lex Julia, the new feature film from Finnish writer and director Laura Hyppönen ( Charlie, Live East Die Young ), which is set on an isolated island and explores such themes as memory and truth.
All sorts of questions come up: Was it a one-night stand or rape? Is she a victim or a coward?

The filmmaker shares that the story “is inspired by a personal experience that took years to distill into a character-driven suspense narrative. I wanted to play with the expectations of the rape-revenge genre: the possibility of violence is constantly present, but the characters find surprising ways to deal with the tension. The film asks whether it is possible to shift deeply held, often unconscious views about sexual violence. Who bears the shame, responsibility and consequences?”

articles.title: Rantzen felt 'deprived of choice' over her own death
articles.summary: A note written by Dame Esther Rantzen is released by her family following a private funeral.
body: A posthumous note written by Dame Esther Rantzen said she was "deprived of any choice over my own death".
The farewell message was released as the 86-year-old broadcaster and campaigner's family confirmed she had been laid to rest in an "incredibly beautiful" private funeral last week.
The Childline founder, who was diagnosed with stage four lung cancer in 2023, died at her Bramshaw home in the New Forest, Hampshire, on 30 September.
A larger memorial service is expected to take place at a later date.
